overview: Seven “List of Papers” index sheets—sheets 35 through 40, including two versions of sheet 39—summarize State Department records from September 1939 through January 1940 concerning Japanese radio interference with American broadcasts and communications. The principal dispute involved reception in East Asia of General Electric station KGEI at Treasure Island and Press Wireless station KJY, allegedly disrupted by Japanese transmitters including JZI, JDK, JND, JZJ, and JZK; the sheets also note Hong Kong station ZBW or ZEN, Japanese propaganda broadcasts, and possible frequency or power changes. The correspondence links the State, Commerce, Navy, and Interior Departments, the Federal Communications Commission, American diplomatic posts in Tokyo, Shanghai, and Batavia, and private radio interests, and records repeated diplomatic representations to Japanese authorities. The final entries extend the problem to interference with U.S. Naval Radio Station NSS and naval direction-finding services.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 35: Initial reports of Japanese radio interference
subfiles.about: Index of September–October 1939 papers concerning suspected Japanese interference with American radio stations and broadcasts in the Pacific and East Asia.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists reports that interference with the Treasure Island station in Java may have originated from Japanese sources and raises the possibility of a protest to Japan. It records technical complaints about the second harmonic of Japanese station JDK interfering with Press Wireless station KJY and about a station believed to be JZI disrupting reception of KGEI. Telegrams from China and Ambassador Grew discuss whether and how to approach Japanese authorities, while also considering protection of Mrs. Frank Williams as the source of information.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, inferred Sheet 36: Shanghai assessment of KGEI reception
subfiles.about: A single-entry index sheet recording the Shanghai American Technical Committee’s conclusion about interference with KGEI reception.
subfiles.summary: The entry summarizes an October 20 telegram from Clarence E. Gauss in Shanghai. The American Technical Committee believed satisfactory reception of Treasure Island station KGEI would remain impossible unless interfering stations ZBW and JZI were eliminated.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 37: KGEI interference and Japanese radio propaganda
subfiles.about: Index of October 1939 communications about Japanese interference with American stations and propaganda broadcasts directed toward the United States.
subfiles.summary: The sheet covers proposed transmission to Tokyo of Shanghai evidence concerning interference by JZI and notes a State Department recommendation not to raise interference attributed to XJOB immediately. Earl Nicholas supplied information about Japanese propaganda stations JZJ and JZK, while the State, Commerce, and Interior Departments and the FCC exchanged inquiries and acknowledgments. Reports from Commercial Attaché Arnold and Consul General Gauss stated that JZI or JZK in Tokyo and ZEN in Hong Kong made reliable Far Eastern reception of KGEI impossible.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 38: Follow-up representations and FCC technical complaints
subfiles.about: Index of October–November 1939 follow-up concerning continued interference with KGEI and KJY and representations made in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Shanghai reported that interference with General Electric’s Treasure Island programs remained severe and asked what remedial efforts were under way; the Department replied that representations made in Tokyo on October 25 were being pursued. FCC Chairman James Lawrence Fly described interference with KJY from JDK’s harmonic and requested comparative signal-strength information from Honolulu and Manila. Further entries record FCC evidence regarding JZI’s off-frequency operation, telegrams to Tokyo, and a Shanghai despatch enclosing press articles and a trade commissioner’s letter.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 39: Late-1939 diplomatic and naval interference cases
subfiles.about: Index of papers extending the radio-interference dispute from KGEI and KJY broadcasts to U.S. naval communications and direction finding.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew forwarded memoranda presented to the Japanese Foreign Office about interference with KGEI and continued to press for a reply. Other entries concern official disapproval of Mrs. Williams’s letter, a Batavia reception chart, and continuing interference with KJY reported by Press Wireless. Navy Department letters asked the State Department to seek elimination of interference by Japanese station JND with Naval Radio Station NSS and by Japanese vessels using the 375-kilocycle direction-finding frequency.

subfiles.title: Duplicate List of Papers, Sheet 39: Expanded late-1939 interference entries
subfiles.about: A duplicate or revised version of sheet 39 providing fuller wording for the KJY, NSS, and naval direction-finding complaints.
subfiles.summary: This sheet repeats the principal entries on Ambassador Grew’s representations over KGEI and on the correspondence involving Mrs. Williams. Its fuller December 22 entry states that Press Wireless regarded interference with KJY as unabated and requested information about relief. It also repeats the Navy Department cases involving JND’s interference with NSS and Japanese vessels operating on 375 kilocycles, followed by instructions to bring the NSS case before Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: List of Papers, Sheet 40: Instructions on naval radio interference
subfiles.about: Index of January 1940 follow-up confirming instructions to protest Japanese interference with American naval communications.
subfiles.summary: The Navy Department was informed that the Embassy in Tokyo had been instructed to make representations about interference caused to Naval Radio Station NSS by Japanese station JND. Ambassador Grew was also instructed to seek elimination of interference with the Naval Communication System’s 375-kilocycle direction-finding service by certain Japanese vessels. A final Navy Department entry acknowledges issuance of that instruction.

interest: The file is useful because it condenses an extended technical and diplomatic dispute into a chronological map of agencies, stations, frequencies, and overseas posts. It shows how ostensibly technical questions—harmonics, off-frequency transmission, power, and signal strength—became entangled with suspicions of deliberate interference and Japanese propaganda on the eve of the Pacific War. The involvement of civilian broadcasters, the FCC, diplomatic missions, and the Navy also reveals how radio-spectrum disputes crossed institutional boundaries. The duplicate versions of sheet 39 are particularly valuable for recovering wording omitted or truncated in one copy and for understanding contemporary filing practices.
